# pandas

![](img/pandas_logo.svg){height="160px" fig-alt="pandas logo"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
wide = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_all.csv")
gapminder = pd.wide_to_long(
    wide, stubnames=["gdpPercap", "lifeExp", "pop"], i="country", j="year", sep="_"
).reset_index()
```

## What is pandas?

:::{.incremental}
* Tables of data, built on NumPy
* **DataFrame**: a table of named columns sharing one row **index**
    * Each column has its own dtype (numbers are NumPy arrays)
* **Series**: one column on its own, with the index
* Reads and writes CSV, Excel, Parquet, SQL, ...
:::

## Reading a CSV file

```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_gdp_europe.csv", index_col="country")
data.head()
```

:::{.incremental}
* `index_col`: the column that becomes the row labels
* `pd.read_excel`, `data.to_csv(...)` for other formats and for writing
:::

## Inspecting a DataFrame

:::{.incremental}
* `data.head()`: the first few rows
* `data.info()`: columns, dtypes, missing values
* `data.describe()`: summary statistics per column
* `data.shape`, `data.columns`, `data.index`
* `data.T`: rows and columns swapped
:::

## Selecting with `iloc` and `loc`

::: {.panel-tabset}

### `iloc`: by position

```{python}
data.iloc[0:2, 0:2].round()
```

* End **excluded**, as in NumPy

### `loc`: by label

```{python}
data.loc["Albania":"Austria", "gdpPercap_1952":"gdpPercap_1957"].round()
```

* End **included**

:::

:::{.incremental}
* `data["gdpPercap_2007"]` is the shortcut for one column
* `:` means "all rows" or "all columns"
:::

## Boolean masks

* The same idea as NumPy masks, but rows keep their labels

```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
rich = data["gdpPercap_2007"] > 40000
data.loc[rich, ["gdpPercap_1952", "gdpPercap_2007"]].round()
```

:::{.incremental}
* Combine conditions with `&`, `|` and `~`, with brackets around each comparison
* `rich.sum()` counts the matching rows; `data[rich]` keeps them
:::

## Group by: split, apply, combine

:::{.incremental}
* **Split** rows into groups by the values in one column
* **Apply** a function to each group: `mean`, `count`, `idxmax`, ...
* **Combine** the results into a table indexed by group
:::

. . .

```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
all_countries = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_all.csv", index_col="country")
all_countries.groupby("continent")["lifeExp_2007"].mean().round(1)
```

::: {.source-note}
Beyond today: missing data and `merge`/`join` are stretch material in the notebook (PDSH chapter 3).
:::

## Live coding: masks and group by {.live-coding}

* Select countries by a condition on one column
* Add a new column computed from others
* Group by continent and summarise
* Several summaries at once with `.agg`

::: {.notes}
```python
all_countries = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_all.csv", index_col="country")
all_countries.head()

long_lived = all_countries["lifeExp_2007"] > 80
long_lived.sum()
all_countries.loc[long_lived, ["continent", "lifeExp_2007"]]

all_countries["lifeExp_gain"] = all_countries["lifeExp_2007"] - all_countries["lifeExp_1952"]
all_countries["lifeExp_gain"].sort_values().tail()

grouped = all_countries.groupby("continent")
grouped["lifeExp_2007"].mean()
grouped["lifeExp_2007"].agg(["count", "median", "max"])
grouped["gdpPercap_2007"].idxmax()     # richest country per continent
grouped["lifeExp_gain"].median().sort_values()
```
:::

# Matplotlib

## Figures, axes and artists

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
t = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
env = np.exp(-t / 3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.6))
ax.plot(t, env * np.sin(2 * t),
        label="signal")
ax.plot(t, env, "--", label="envelope")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_title("One Figure, one Axes")
ax.legend();
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{.incremental}
* **Figure**: the whole canvas, saved to a file
* **Axes**: one plot area; a figure can hold many
* **Artists**: everything drawn (lines, text, ticks), each with properties you can change
:::
:::
::::

## `pyplot` versus `fig, ax`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**pyplot style**: acts on the "current" axes

```python
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
**Object-oriented style**: says which axes

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::
::::

<br>

:::{.incremental}
* You used `fig, ax` yesterday; we use it throughout: it scales to many panels and works inside functions
* Most `plt.xlabel(...)` calls become `ax.set_xlabel(...)`
* Code from an LLM or the web often mixes the two: settle on one before you change it
:::

::: {.source-note}
Matplotlib docs, [the two interfaces](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/figure/api_interfaces.html).
:::

## Saving figures

```python
fig.savefig("figure.pdf")                                # vector: line plots, for papers
fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")  # raster: images, slides
```

:::{.incremental}
* The extension picks the format
* `bbox_inches="tight"` trims the white border
:::

## Plots from an LLM

:::{.incremental}
* Fine for a first draft: you rarely need to remember `ax.spines[...]` or `annotate` arguments
* **Ask well:** the shape and dtype of your arrays or the columns of your DataFrame, units, the message of the plot; ask for `fig, ax` code
* **Read before you run:** which data goes on which axis, and which `ax` each line changes
* **Check what you see:**
    * Axis labels **with units**; limits that do not hide data
    * Colormap: sequential for magnitudes, diverging only for data centred on zero
    * Images: `origin`, `aspect` and `extent`
    * Legend entries that match the lines
* The figure carries your name, not the LLM's
:::

## Live coding: a first figure {.live-coding}

* Plot a damped oscillation with the defaults
* Improve it: size, colours, labels, legend; save it as PNG and PDF
* The same plot in `pyplot` style, then translate it back to `fig, ax`

::: {.notes}
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

t = np.linspace(0, 10, 500)
signal = np.exp(-t / 3) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, signal)                           # defaults

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(t, signal, color="black", linewidth=1, label="signal")
ax.plot(t, np.exp(-t / 3), "--", color="tab:orange", label="envelope")
ax.set_xlim(0, 8)
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
ax.set_title("A damped oscillation")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")

fig.savefig("damped.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("damped.pdf")

plt.plot(t, signal)                          # pyplot style
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::

## More plot types

| Method | For |
|---|---|
| `ax.scatter(x, y, s=..., c=...)` | Points, with size and colour per point |
| `ax.hist(values, bins=...)` | Distributions |
| `ax.bar(names, heights)` | Values per category |
| `ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=...)` | Means with error bars |
| `ax.imshow(array)` | Images and 2-D arrays |

. . .

* Several panels: `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3)`, then `axes[0].plot(...)`

## Images and colormaps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
moon = plt.imread("data/moonlanding.png")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2,
                         figsize=(5, 2))
axes[0].imshow(moon)
axes[1].imshow(moon, cmap="gray")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_axis_off()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::{.incremental}
* A 2-D grey image has no colour: `imshow` maps values through a **colormap**
* Perceptually uniform maps (`viridis`, `gray`); diverging maps (`RdBu_r`) only for data centred on zero
* `fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)` shows the mapping
:::
:::
::::

## Statistical plots from DataFrames

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| output: false
import seaborn as sns

y2007 = gapminder.query("year == 2007")
sns.relplot(
    data=y2007,
    x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
    hue="continent", size="pop",
    sizes=(10, 600),
).set(xscale="log")
```

::: {.incremental}
* Each argument maps a **column** to a visual property
* Legends, colours and sizes come for free
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%" .fragment fragment-index=1}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
g = sns.relplot(
    data=gapminder.query("year == 2007"),
    x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", hue="continent", size="pop",
    sizes=(10, 600), alpha=0.7, height=4, aspect=1.3,
)
g.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita (log)", ylabel="Life expectancy")
sns.reset_orig()
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 11})
```
:::
::::

## When to reach for seaborn

:::{.incremental}
* **seaborn:** a tidy DataFrame; colour, size or panels by category; means with confidence intervals; distributions
* **Plain Matplotlib:** arrays and images, custom layouts, unusual plot types
* seaborn draws **with** Matplotlib: `ax=`, `fig.savefig` and the last block still apply
:::

# scikit-learn

## What is scikit-learn?

:::{.incremental}
* Machine learning in Python, built on NumPy and SciPy
* **Supervised**: learn to predict `y` from `X` (classification, regression)
* **Unsupervised**: find structure in `X` alone (clustering, dimensionality reduction)
* Every model has the **same interface**: learn it once
:::

## `X` and `y`

:::{.incremental}
* `X`: a table, **one row per sample**, **one column per feature**
    * A DataFrame or a 2-D NumPy array
    * Here: one row per trial; `trials[["contrast", "probability_left"]]`
* `y`: a 1-D array, one answer per sample
    * Here: did the mouse choose right?
* `X` must be 2-D even with one feature: `trials[["contrast"]]`, not `trials["contrast"]`
:::

## The estimator pattern

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
hours = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(100, 1))     # X: 100 x 1
passed = hours[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 2, 100) > 5   # y

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(hours, passed)
model.predict([[2.0], [8.0]])
```

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| output-location: fragment
model.predict_proba([[2.0], [8.0]]).round(2)
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
:::{.incremental}
* **Make** the model, with its settings
* **`fit(X, y)`** learns from the data
* **`predict(X)`** for new samples
* **`predict_proba(X)`**: one column per class, in the order of `model.classes_`
* Learned values end in `_`: `model.coef_`
:::
:::
::::

## Train and test

:::{.incremental}
* A model scored on the data it learned from looks better than it is
* Hold some samples back: **fit** on the training set, **score** on the test set
* Compare with a **baseline**, such as always guessing the most common answer
* **Cross-validation** repeats the split several ways: `cross_val_score`
:::

. . .

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
model.score(X_test, y_test)          # fraction correct
```

## Live coding: hours of study {.live-coding}

* The pass/fail data from the slide: split, fit, score
* Compare with the baseline
* `coef_`, then `predict_proba` on a grid, plotted over the data

::: {.notes}
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
hours = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(100, 1))
passed = hours[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 2, 100) > 5
hours.shape, passed.shape

h_train, h_test, p_train, p_test = train_test_split(hours, passed, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression().fit(h_train, p_train)
model.score(h_train, p_train), model.score(h_test, p_test)
max(p_test.mean(), 1 - p_test.mean())      # baseline

model.coef_, model.intercept_, model.classes_
grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 101)[:, np.newaxis]   # 2-D!
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hours[:, 0], passed, "o", alpha=0.4)
ax.plot(grid[:, 0], model.predict_proba(grid)[:, 1])
```
:::

# Where to go next

## scikit-image: images are arrays

```python
import skimage as ski

image = ski.io.imread("nuclei.tif")                  # a NumPy array
smooth = ski.filters.gaussian(image, sigma=2)
mask = smooth > ski.filters.threshold_otsu(smooth)   # a boolean mask
labels = ski.measure.label(mask)                     # 0 = background, 1..N = objects
table = ski.measure.regionprops_table(labels, properties=["area", "eccentricity"])
```

:::{.incremental}
* **Use it when:** you filter, threshold, segment or measure microscopy (or any) images
* Measurements come out as a table, ready for pandas and seaborn
:::

::: {.source-note}
[scikit-image.org/docs/stable/user_guide](https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/user_guide.html); SPL, [scikit-image: image processing](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/packages/scikit-image/index.html)
:::

## xarray: labelled N-D arrays

```python
import xarray as xr

lfp = xr.DataArray(lfp_uv, dims=("time", "channel"),
                   coords={"time": time, "area": ("channel", area)})
lfp.sel(time=slice(2, 4)).mean(dim="time")   # by label and by name, not position
lfp.groupby("area").mean()
```

:::{.incremental}
* **Use it when:** you keep forgetting which axis is time, or carry coordinates (seconds, µm, brain areas) alongside your arrays
* Reads and writes NetCDF and Zarr; pandas-style `groupby` on N-D data
:::

::: {.source-note}
[tutorial.xarray.dev](https://tutorial.xarray.dev)
:::

## dask: bigger than memory, in parallel

```python
import dask.array as da

with h5py.File("big_recording.h5") as f:
    lfp = da.from_array(f["lfp/data"], chunks=(100_000, 384))   # lazy: nothing read yet
    channel_std = lfp.std(axis=0)                               # NumPy code, still lazy
    result = channel_std.compute()                              # runs, chunk by chunk, on all cores
```

:::{.incremental}
* **Use it when:** your data do not fit in memory, or one core is too slow
* NumPy- and pandas-like interfaces; xarray uses it under the hood
:::

::: {.source-note}
[tutorial.dask.org](https://tutorial.dask.org)
:::

## napari: look at your data

```python
import napari

viewer = napari.Viewer()
viewer.add_image(image, name="nuclei")
viewer.add_labels(labels, name="segmentation")
edited = viewer.layers["segmentation"].data          # read your edits back as an array
```

:::{.incremental}
* **Use it when:** you need to browse, check or annotate N-D images: z-stacks, time-lapses, many channels
* Opens a desktop window: install it on your own machine
:::

::: {.source-note}
[napari.org/stable/tutorials](https://napari.org/stable/tutorials/)
:::

## Also worth knowing

| Package | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **statsmodels** | Regression models and statistical tests with full summary tables |
| **pingouin** | Common statistical tests on DataFrames, with effect sizes |
| **Zarr** | Chunked, compressed N-D arrays on disk or in the cloud |
| **Polars** | Fast DataFrames with a lazy query engine |
| **Numba** | Compiles the Python loops you cannot avoid to machine code with `@numba.njit` |
